To obtain the steering vectors, we follow Wang et al. (2025). They find that, on several out-of-context-reasoning tasks, a LoRA finetune behaves like the addition of one constant vector and that such a vector can be trained from scratch to reproduce the behavior introduced by the finetune. We initialize a random vector and add it to the output of one layer’s MLP block before the output re-enters the residual stream. The vector is added at the last prompt token only. The loss is a masked causal-LM loss over the teacher-forced answer. The vectors are trained on labeled task data. #### Nonlinear mapping from a random MLP. For the task of learning the outputs of a random MLP, we first evaluate all layers for one epoch. We select the best performing layer 14, then tune the learning rate and the training length. The best vector trains for 16 epochs at a learning rate of $3.2\times 10^{-2}$ with 8-bit Adam and an effective batch size of 64.

At epoch 16, they produce French on average $23.5\%$ of the time for trained female-name prompts, compared with $0.0\%$ for male-name and no-name prompts (Figure˜7). The behavior also generalizes beyond the teacher’s training distribution: students produce French on $20.2\%$ of prompts with held-out female names and $17.3\%$ of prompts using the held-out template. The strength of the effect varies substantially across seeds: for trained female names, individual rates range from $15.0\%$ to $38.8\%$ between students. Transfer also depends strongly on the LoRA configuration (see Appendix˜D). #### Transfer via sampled tokens. The backdoor also transfers without the teacher’s next-token distributions. We extend the transfer dataset from 90,000 to 4.5 million number-sequence rows. A student finetuned on the teacher’s sampled tokens from this dataset answers in French on $8.5\%$ of trained female-name prompts at its last checkpoint and on $17.0\%$ two checkpoints earlier, against $0.0\%$ for male-name and no-name prompts (Figure˜7(b)).

Write-up text before the decision: hack. ## 8 Discussion #### Subliminal transfer of misalignment. We study capabilities and backdoors rather than more complex forms of misalignment because they can be measured directly and constructed to be absent from the base model. Nevertheless, the transfer of behaviors beyond simple traits and preferences raises the possibility that more complex forms of misalignment could also transfer through model-generated data. Moreover, the stronger transfer we observe for an existing capability (Section˜3) suggests that subliminal learning may amplify behaviors that are already present in a model. #### Relation to the steering-vector distillation hypothesis. Blank et al. (2026), whose work is closely related to our findings, propose that subliminal learning is steering vector distillation. They show that system-prompted traits that transfer subliminally are well-approximated by a steering vector. Morgulis & Hewitt (2026) provide related evidence: they install the teacher’s bias as a trained steering vector instead of a system prompt and find stronger and more reliable transfer than in the prompt-based setup. In Section˜4, we find that none of the tested system prompts reproduce either the random MLP mapping or the letter counting capability. In Section˜5, we therefore test whether a directly optimized steering vector added to a single layer can reproduce the capability acquired by the student. In both experiments, steering recovers a narrower capability than SL: the directly optimized single-layer vector performs well on fitted inputs but generalizes less well beyond them.

Problem: How strongly to state the paper's conclusion given weak and setup-sensitive transfer
Write-up text before the decision: transfer in SL, including divergence tokens and early layers (Schrodi et al., 2026), alignment between teacher and student (Okatan et al., 2025; Brockers et al., 2026), non-semantic structure in the weights (Hadley & Gultepe, 2026), and the strength of the teacher’s bias (König et al., 2026). However, these studies mostly concern simple traits. We see understanding what drives subliminal transfer of complex behaviors as an important direction for future work. #### Limitations. Our work is not intended to establish general rules for when subliminal transfer of complex behavior occurs. Rather, we show evidence that such transfer is possible. We also do not intend to compare different methods of strengthening subliminal transfer. Our settings also differ from the original setup of Cloud et al. (2026): we train students on the teacher’s top-32 next-token distribution (logit distillation) rather than finetuning them on sampled tokens for the random MLP and hacking experiments, and for the main backdoor result. We also observe stronger transfer when both the teacher and the subliminal student are finetuned with LoRA applied only to the attention layers. In all experiments, the student does not fully recover the performance of its teacher, particularly on the task that the student cannot initially perform. Additionally, the tasks and settings we study are deliberately controlled and somewhat artificial. This is especially true for random MLP regression.
